abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Slash is a waste product generated from commercial forestry operations. In 2022, flooding slash caused devastating damage when Cyclone Gabrielle directly impacted the Hawke's Bay region of New Zealand. This study addresses the dual challenges of waste management and sustainable materials development by converting forestry slash into high‐performance carbon electrodes through an innovative in situ sulfur doping process. Building upon prior research involving waste‐derived materials, this study develops a hydrothermal sulfurization technique that transforms New Zealand slash into sulfur‐doped, highly graphitized carbon materials with excellent energy storage properties. The hydrothermally sulfurized slash‐derived electrode material (C‐HS‐New Zealand Slash (NZS)) exhibits a high specific capacitance of 148 F g− 1 at a current density of 0.5 A g− 1. A supercapacitor device assembles with the C‐HS‐NZS electrode achieves a capacitance of 440 F g− 1 at the same current density. The energy density reaches 15.3 Wh kg− 1 at a power density of 250 W kg− 1. Furthermore, the C‐HS‐NZS‐based device delivers a maximum capacitance of 384 F g− 1 and retains 360 F g− 1 after 10,000 cycles, demonstrating excellent capacity retention and long‐term electrochemical stability.

sec.p: Keywords: biomass‐derived carbon, sulfur doping, supercapacitors, waste management, waste woody materials

abstract.p: This study transforms forestry slash waste into high‐performance sulfur‐doped carbon electrodes via hydrothermal sulfurization. The resulting material (C‐HS‐New Zealand Slash (NZS)) exhibits high capacitance (148 F g− 1) and energy density (15.3 Wh kg− 1). Supercapacitors with C‐HS‐NZS electrodes retain 360 F g− 1 after 10,000 cycles, offering a sustainable solution for waste management and energy storage.

sec.p: Revised 2025 Apr 7; Received 2025 Feb 25; Issue date 2025 Jul 1.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In the present research, we have designed two stages in situ sulfur doping processes to enhance the electrochemical performance of treated carbon materials from New Zealand Slash (NZS). Slash primarily consists of lignocellulosic biomass, which is rich in carbon and can be converted into porous carbon materials through processes such as pyrolysis, chemical activation, and hydrothermal carbonization. These processes break down the complex organic structure of the biomass, removing noncarbon elements and creating a highly porous carbon framework. Compared with carbon sources derived from fossil fuel, utilizing NZS as a precursor for carbon materials leverages its abundant availability and low cost, addressing both waste management and the need for sustainable carbon sources in one innovative approach. By converting this biomass waste into valuable carbon‐based materials, we can mitigate the environmental issues associated with logging debris and simultaneously contribute to the development of clean energy technologies. This study demonstrates that the pretreatment method employed can enhance the graphitization degree of the derived carbon, optimize its structural order and significantly improve electronic conductivity, thereby enhancing the overall performance of supercapacitors. The influence of in situ doping methods on the efficiency of sulfur incorporation and the resultant changes in the chemical structure of the biomass‐derived carbon material were investigated and discussed.

sec.title: Experimental Section
sec.p: Inspired by previous research, we utilized concentrated sulfuric acid with two distinct sulfurization processing methods, namely soaking (S‐) and hydrothermal (HS‐) treatments, to prepare precursors from NZS, thereby obtaining S‐doped carbon in‐place.

sec.title: Raw Materials
sec.p: The NZS materials were delivered by our commercial cooperator, which collected by a local forestry company in the East Coast region of New Zealand. Concentrated sulfuric acid (H2SO4) was obtained from Merck (95–97% H2SO4, analytic grade). Potassium hydroxide (≥85% KOH, ACS reagent) was obtained from Sigma–Aldrich. Nickel foams (NFs), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and 1‐methyl‐2‐pyrrolidone (NMP) were gained from MTI Corp.

sec.title: Synthesis Method
sec.p: Initially, 15 g of NZS were cleaned with distilled water and ethanol to remove impurities. The barks were then divided into three batches for further treatment. The first batch was immersed in distilled water and stirred for 24 h, designated as NZS. The second batch was soaked in concentrated H2SO4 for 24 h, referred to as S‐NZS (sulfurized NZS). The third batch underwent a two‐step process: It was soaked in concentrated H2SO4 for 12 h, followed by hydrothermal treatment at 100 °C in H2SO4 solution for an additional 12 h, labeled as HS‐NZS (hydrothermally sulfurized NZS).

After rinsing and drying, all samples were subjected to carbonization at 900 °C in a tube furnace under an argon atmosphere for 9 h. The resulting carbonized samples were named C‐NZS (carbonized NZS), C‐S‐NZS (carbonized S‐NZS), and C‐HS‐NZS (carbonized HS‐NZS). Figure 1 illustrates the schematic of the experimental procedure.

caption.p: The experimental schematic description for the synthesis of different NZS‐derived carbon materials.

sec.title: Materials Characterizations
sec.p: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA, Shimadzu TA‐50) was performed to measure the carbon yield rate after various pretreatment methods, heating up to 900 °C at a rate of 10 °C min− 1 under argon gas protection. The morphology and microstructures of NZS, C‐NZS, C‐S‐NZS, and C‐HS‐NZS were analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, HITACHI SU70) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL, JEM‐2100F). Elemental compositions were determined using the attached energy‐dispersive spectrometer (EDS, BRUKER XFlash 6‐30). The phase structure of the samples was examined by X‐ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Ultima IV) with Cu Kα radiation at 40 kV and 200 mA. Raman spectroscopy (HORIBA LabRAM HR Evolution) and Fourier‐transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, ThermoFisher Nicolet iS50) were employed to further characterize the chemical structure of the synthesized materials. Surface composition analysis was conducted using X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ThermoFisher Nexsa).

sec.title: Electrochemical Measurement
sec.p: A slurry for the working electrode was prepared by mixing NMP solvent with a compound of carbonized material powder and PVDF in a mass ratio of 9:1. This slurry was then applied onto NFs and subsequently dried in an oven at 60 °C for 12 h to complete the fabrication of the working electrodes. The performance of the working electrode was evaluated using a three‐electrode system. The C‐HS‐NZS samples were used as the active material in a coin‐cell‐type symmetric supercapacitor (SSC). The device was assembled with two NF discs (12 mm in diameter), each loaded with 1.2 mg of active material, and a 16 mm glass fiber separator. The average total thickness of the prepared electrode (including active material and nickel foam) was 0.101 mm.

The three‐electrode system was tested in the 6 M KOH liquid electrolyte through an electrochemical workstation (CHI 660E, USA) under ambient temperature, using a Hg/HgO electrode as the reference electrode and a 10 × 10 mm2 platinum (Pt) plate as the counter electrode. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed to characterize the property of treated NZS with an applied voltage of (−1 to 0) V at a scan rate range of (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, and 200) mV s− 1. Galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) was employed between −1 and 0 V in a various current density range (0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10 A g− 1) to study the capacity ability. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was executed in a 10 mV AC signal amplitude with the frequency spectrum start from 0.01 to 100,000 Hz.

sec.title: NZS Materials Analysis

sec.p: Figure 3 illustrates the growth morphology of NZS, C‐NZS, C‐S‐NZS, and C‐HS‐NZS samples characterized by a SEM/EDS. The raw NZS show a large particle of macroscopic size with many pores as given in Figure 3a. Following carbonization, the untreated NZS largely retained the morphology of raw NZS. However, some porosity was introduced due to the thermal treatment process. The C‐S‐NZS and C‐HS‐NZS samples that underwent sulfurization experienced a degradation of their original morphology, forming an aggregated morphology of microscopic spheroidal particles without obvious size differences (Figure 3c,d). The EDS mapping images of C‐HS‐NZS (Figure 3e) display a comparatively homogeneous allocation of C, O, and S elements, which proves that S atoms were doped into the C‐HS‐NZS sample successfully.

sec.title: Electrochemical Characterization via Three‐Electrode Configuration
sec.p: Figure 5a shows the CV curves for C‐NZS, C‐S‐NZS, and C‐HS‐NZS at a sweep rate of 10 mV s− 1, exhibiting a nearly rectangular shape between −1 and 0 V, characteristic of classical EDLC storage behavior. Typically, a larger area enclosed by the CV curve at a constant scanning rate correlates with an increased specific capacitance of the electrode material based on the Equation (1). The C‐HS‐NZS sample had the highest response current, and its rectangular area was the largest one so that C‐HS‐NZS had a higher specific capacitance compare to C‐NZS and C‐S‐NZS. The CV performance of C‐HS‐NZS samples was tested at a scan rate of 1–200 mV s− 1 (Figure 5b), showing the capacitance of 175 F g− 1 using the scanning speed of 1 mV s− 1. CV curves of C‐HS‐NZS has the similar rectangular shapes at different scan rates, which means the sample has an excellent rate capability. The capacitive performance of carbonized NZS materials was further evaluated by GCD measurement. Figure 5c is the GCD graphs of NZS‐derived carbon electrodes at the current density of 1 A g− 1, showing nearly isosceles triangular shapes. This indicates that carbonized NZS electrodes store energy through the double‐layer capacitor mechanism. Under a fixed current density, sulfurized carbon materials notably exhibit longer charge–discharge times compared to untreated carbon materials, suggesting higher capacitance in the sulfurized samples.

sec.title: Symmetric Supercapacitor
sec.p: The coin cell‐type symmetric supercapacitor is assembled by using the C‐HS‐NZS electrode and a 6 M KOH aqueous electrolyte with an electrochemical stability operation voltage of 0 to 1 V (Figure 7 ). The quasirectangular CV curve at varied scanning speeds (1–200 mV s− 1) in Figure 7a and the GCD curve in Figure 7b at different current densities (0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10 A g− 1) approximating the isosceles triangle exhibit outstanding rate performance with the main energy storage mechanism of double‐layer capacitance. Figure 7c summarizes the capacitance changes at diverse current densities. Its specific capacitance was 440 F g− 1 at 0.5 A g− 1 and kept at 380 F g− 1 about 86% capacity retention at a high current density of 10 A g− 1.

Figure 7d shows the Ragone plots (energy density and power density, calculated by Equation (4) and (5)) by comparing the fabricated supercapacitor with previously reported supercapacitors depend on biomass‐derived carbon electrodes, showing promising for energy storage applications. The power density of the SSC based on C‐HS‐NZS electrodes is 250 W kg− 1 at an energy density of 15.3 Wh kg− 1. When the current density increased to 10 A g− 1, the energy density is still as high as 13.2 Wh kg− 1 at a power density of 5.3 kW kg− 1. The Ragone Plots demonstrating this fabricated SSC is comparable with the previously reported supercapacitors based on other biomass derived carbon materials, as illustrated in Table 1 .

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This work in situ successfully synthesized S‐doped carbon derived from NZS through different sulfurization processes. Sulfurization process can improve the carbon yield rate; and the hydrothermal sulfurization treatment boosts the graphitization degree of this biomass‐derived carbon and, meanwhile, introduces sulfuric atoms into carbon frame. Due to the high graphitization, C‐HS‐NZS electrode material achieves outstanding capacitances of 175 F g− 1 when the scanning rate is 1 mV s− 1, or 148 F g− 1 at the current density of 0.5 A g− 1, and a superior inner resistance of 0.6 Ω. The device assembled by the C‐HS‐NZS electrode has an excellent rate performance and outstanding storage capacity of 440 F g− 1 at 0.5 A g− 1. Moreover, the symmetric supercapacitor device assembled with the C‐HS‐NZS electrode exhibits a high capacitance retention of 86% at 10 A g− 1. The energy density can reach 15.3 Wh kg− 1 when power density is 250 W kg− 1. After 10,000 cycles GCD test under a high current density of 10 A g− 1, the coin cell symmetrical supercapacitor of C‐HS‐NZS shows excellent stability with almost 100% coulombic efficient, illustrating an impressive application potential. This study demonstrates that the sulfurization‐treated carbonized NZS materials exhibit superior electrochemical performance is attributed to the sulfurization process, which promotes graphitization while simultaneously introducing heteroatom doping. Hydrothermal sulfurization treatment could improve the graphitization degree more efficiently than only soaking in H2SO4.
